lessons.title: The Problem Timeline
body: A customer's problem rarely starts the moment they go looking for a solution. It usually exists before they ever search for anything, continues while they're trying to solve it on their own or with the wrong tools, and — more often than beginners expect — part of it is still there after they get an initial result. The Problem Timeline splits this into three stages — Before, During and After — so your offer matches the customer's real experience, not just the moment they click “buy.”

Before — the situation before they look for a solution
Four questions are worth asking about every candidate problem here: what actually triggers the customer to start looking for help, what frustrations or obstacles they're already dealing with, what they currently can't do that they want to be able to do, and what happens if they do nothing at all. That last question matters more than it looks — a problem people can comfortably ignore forever is a much weaker Before than one with a real cost to inaction.

During — the difficulties they hit while trying to solve it
This is everything that goes wrong between deciding to act and actually getting a result — and it's the stage beginners skip most often, because it's about the struggle in the middle, not the starting point or the finish line. Look for what makes the process genuinely difficult, what causes confusion or frustration along the way, which existing solutions turn out to be inadequate once someone actually tries them, what specific mistakes or obstacles show up, and what makes people abandon the process partway through. A During problem you can remove is often the fastest win available to you, because it doesn't require inventing a new outcome — only clearing friction from a path the customer has already chosen.

After — what they want once the problem is solved
After describes a destination, not a feature list. Ask what the customer actually wants to achieve, what would become easier once they get there, what result would make the whole effort worthwhile, and what practical or emotional improvement they're really after. It's worth saying plainly: After is not “gets access to 12 video lessons” — that's a thing your product does. After is the change in the customer's life or work those lessons are supposed to produce. Keep rewriting an After entry until it describes the customer, not the product.

Where this evidence comes from
Module 1 already taught you how to find real evidence about your market. The Problem Timeline doesn't ask you to go research again — it asks you to look at what you already collected, through a different lens:
  • Open your research log from Lesson 1.2 and reread it end to end, rather than relying on memory.
  • Revisit the actual source discussions for anything that stood out, instead of working from your summary of them.
  • Extract the real complaints and desired outcomes, written as close to the customer's own words as you can.
  • Group observations that are clearly describing the same underlying problem, even if the wording differs.
  • Place each grouped problem into Before, During or After, based on when it happens in the customer's experience.
If a stage comes up empty, that's a signal to go back and look again — not an invitation to invent a plausible-sounding problem to fill the gap. A stage built from guesses will mislead every module that builds on it later.

Vague feelings vs. specific problems
Most beginners write their first problem statements as vague feelings rather than specific, evidenced problems. The fix is almost always the same: replace a general feeling with the precise thing the customer is struggling with, stated the way they’d actually say it — for example, a hypothetical small business owner who struggles to create consistent social media content:
VAGUE
“I want to grow my business on social media.”
SPECIFIC
“I have a small business, but I struggle to come up with content ideas and create posts consistently.”
The second version is usable. It tells you exactly what’s broken (generating ideas and staying consistent), which stage it belongs to (During — it surfaces while the owner is already trying to post), and roughly what a solution would need to do. Here’s the same owner’s problem carried across all three stages — this is the example used throughout the rest of this module:
BEFORE — “I know I need to post regularly, but I often have no idea what to post or where to start.”
DURING — “I spend hours creating social media posts, but struggle with the designs, captions and deciding what content will actually be useful.”
AFTER — “I want to plan and create a week’s worth of social media content without spending hours figuring out what to post every day.”
These are hypothetical teaching examples, not actual customer quotations or verified research. The same distinction holds well outside social media — a hypothetical freelancer managing several client projects might state a During problem as “I start each project with a clear plan, but by the second week I’m juggling revisions across three clients with no system to track what’s due when,” which is specific enough to design a product around, where “client management is hard” is not.
lessons.insight: Understanding all three stages matters because most beginners only design for one — usually the moment right before the sale. A product that also addresses a real During friction or leaves the customer somewhere better After tends to feel like it was built by someone who understands the whole journey, not just the transaction.

lessons.title: From Problems to Opportunities
body: By now your Problem Inventory should be taking shape across Before, During and After. Not every problem on that list belongs in the same place in your offer. This lesson teaches you to sort them into two categories: the one problem your core product must solve, and the problems better handled as bonuses — or sometimes, not addressed by you at all.

Core product problem vs. bonus problem
Core product problem: the problem directly connected to the main reason the customer would buy. If this problem isn't solved, the product fails to deliver its central value — everything else is secondary. Bonus problem: a related, secondary problem that improves the customer's experience but isn't essential to the main transformation. Solving it adds polish; failing to solve it doesn't sink the product. Adding too many unrelated bonuses does real damage to an offer — it makes the core promise harder to see, raises production time without raising conviction, and signals to the customer that you weren't sure what the product was actually for.

A practical sorting test
Run each candidate problem through these questions, roughly in order:
  • Is this the main problem the customer came to solve? It belongs in the core deliverable.
  • Does it support the main outcome but remain secondary? It may become a bonus.
  • Can it be created as a useful, focused add-on within a few hours? It's often suitable as a bonus.
  • Does it require substantial development, or solve a separate major problem of its own? It may deserve to be its own product, or a core component — not a bonus.
Important: don't treat the “a few hours” guideline as an absolute law. A bonus that takes a weekend to build but directly removes a painful During obstacle can be worth it; a bonus you could build in an hour but that has nothing to do with the customer's actual outcome usually isn't worth including at all. Relevance to the outcome matters more than production time alone.

A complete worked example — hypothetical
Continuing with the hypothetical small business owner from Lesson 2.1, who struggles to create consistent social media content:
MAIN CUSTOMER PROBLEM
“I have a small business, but I struggle to come up with content ideas and create posts consistently.”
CORE DELIVERABLE
A content planning system that turns one sitting into a full week of ready-to-post social media content.
SUPPLEMENTARY PROBLEMS → POSSIBLE BONUSES
Running out of caption ideas → a caption prompt swipe file. Posts looking inconsistent from one to the next → a small set of brand-consistent post templates. Forgetting which posts actually performed well → a simple one-page tracking sheet.
Each bonus earns its place because it’s a direct, minor extension of the same core problem — captions, visual consistency and tracking are all small, natural companions to “planning and creating a week of content” itself. Something that should not be added as a bonus here is a full auto-posting and analytics tool: it solves a genuinely different problem (distribution and scheduling, not content creation), and it’s substantial enough to be its own product — bolting it on as a “free bonus” would quietly double the development work while diluting what the offer is actually promising.

Sorting your own inventory
  • Review the problems you collected in Lesson 2.1.
  • Identify the problem most directly connected to the desired outcome — the After your customer is actually paying for.
  • Mark it as your potential core problem.
  • Group the problems closely related to it.
  • Identify secondary problems that could meaningfully improve the experience without being essential.
  • Assign suitable problems to potential bonuses, using the sorting test above.
  • Remove anything left over that's unrelated or too small to matter — not every noticed problem needs a place in this offer.
The objective is a focused product, not a collection of random features.
lessons.insight: A strong offer is not necessarily the offer with the most deliverables. A single core problem solved completely, with one or two well-matched bonuses, usually outsells a crowded stack of loosely related extras — because the customer can see exactly what they're buying and why it fits them.

lessons.title: Your Problem Inventory
body: The worksheet below is where your Problem Inventory actually gets built — one entry per real customer problem, sorted into Before, During and After. Before you start typing, it's worth knowing how to tell a problem worth keeping from one that isn't.

One-off complaints vs. recurring problems
One-off complaint: a problem mentioned by one person, in one particular situation, that may not reflect anyone else's experience. Recurring problem: a similar difficulty appearing independently across multiple people or sources, even when they describe it in different words. Recurring problems deserve more of your attention, because they're more likely to still be there when you launch. Look for repeated language, similar frustrations expressed differently, the same failed solutions showing up again, common obstacles, and similar desired outcomes across people who don't know each other. None of this is a precise science — there's no specific number of mentions that proves real market demand — but a problem you've seen independently three or four times is on much firmer ground than one you only noticed once.

A completed example — hypothetical
A finished Problem Inventory for the hypothetical small business owner from earlier in this module might look like this. Notice that every After entry describes something the customer can now do or feel — not a feature of the product:
BeforeDuringAfter
Knows social media matters for the business but has no clear plan for what to post or when.Spends hours each week trying to come up with post ideas and often ends up skipping days entirely.Can sit down once a week and leave with a full week of content ready to publish.
Has tried posting whenever inspiration strikes, with no repeatable process behind it.Keeps rewriting captions because nothing sounds right, which eats up most of the time spent on content.Feels confident posting captions that sound like their brand without rewriting every one from scratch.
Relies on whatever design tool is free that day, so nothing looks connected to the last post.Has no simple way to keep designs looking consistent from one post to the next.Has a repeatable system for turning one idea into a finished, on-brand post.

How to complete the exercise below
  • Return to your Lesson 1.2 research log rather than working from memory.
  • Select the observations that actually relate to this market and offer idea.
  • Rewrite each one as a single, specific sentence a real customer would say — not a category label like “motivation issues.”
  • Place it in Before, During or After, based on when it happens in the customer's experience.
  • Before adding a new entry, scan what you've already written — if it's really the same problem in different words, strengthen the existing entry instead of duplicating it.
  • Ask yourself whether the entry is something you actually found, or something you're assuming is probably true — if you can't point to where it came from, it's an assumption, not a problem yet.
  • Keep at least two meaningful, specific problems in each stage.
A good finished inventory reads like a set of things real people said, grouped by when they happen — not a brainstorm of everything that might conceivably go wrong.

Where this inventory goes next
This inventory is the foundation for the rest of Offer Engineering. In Module 3, you'll use it to decide exactly which problems and outcomes your offer should address. In Module 4, the core problem you identify in Lesson 2.2 becomes your main deliverable, and the secondary problems shape your bonuses. In Module 5, how important the problem is — and how much it costs the customer to stay stuck — feeds directly into your pricing hypothesis. And in Module 6, the strongest problem and desired outcome you've written here help shape how you name and position the finished product.
lessons.insight: A Problem Inventory is only as useful as the evidence behind it. One built from repeated, real customer language will keep paying off through every module that follows; one built from assumptions will need to be rebuilt the moment it meets a real customer.

exercise.instructions: Add at least two problems to each stage before continuing — a thin inventory produces a thin offer.

prompt.title: Problem Inventory Prompt
prompt.purpose: Use this to surface problems you wouldn't have thought to list yourself.
prompt.template: You are a customer-research analyst helping someone list every problem their future customer has, not just the obvious one, organised using DigitalOps's Problem Timeline — Before, During and After. My target customer: {{m1.topMarket}}. My intended offer area: {{m0.path}}. Give me 5 Before problems (what's happening before this customer looks for a solution), 5 During problems (what goes wrong while they're trying to solve it), and 5 After problems (what's still unresolved once they get an initial result) — each written as one plain sentence a real customer would say, not a category label. If my target customer or offer area above is too vague to generate real, specific problems, tell me what's missing and ask me to clarify before listing anything. For every problem, mark whether it's something most people in this situation would plausibly experience, or something that only holds under a specific assumption about this customer I haven't actually stated — flag the assumption explicitly rather than presenting it as fact. Don't invent statistics or cite made-up research — reason only from ordinary common sense about this situation. These are AI-generated candidates, not verified market research: once you've given me the list, remind me to check each one against my own Module 1 research log and mark which ones I can actually confirm I observed, versus which are just plausible guesses I still need to validate.
